title: Regulated vs Offshore: Canada's Channelization Fight
excerpt: Channelization is the number Canadian regulators care most about. Here is what it measures, why it is so hard to move, and what it means for players.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Ask a Canadian gambling regulator what success looks like and you will not hear about revenue. You will hear about channelization — the share of money wagered by residents that flows through licensed, regulated operators rather than offshore sites beyond any provincial authority. It is an unglamorous word for the central question of Canadian iGaming policy, and four years into Ontario's open market it is the metric that determines whether the whole experiment is judged a success.

Channelization also happens to be the concept that explains most of what players notice about the Canadian market: why regulated sites impose limits that offshore ones do not, why advertising rules keep tightening, and why provinces keep arriving at slightly different answers to the same problem. This piece explains how the measure works, why it is harder to move than it looks, and what it actually means for someone deciding where to play.

What channelization measures

In principle the calculation is simple: take all the money residents of a jurisdiction gamble online, and work out what proportion of it goes to operators the jurisdiction licenses. A high figure means the regulated market has captured the demand. A low figure means players are still using sites that answer to nobody local, where regulators have no visibility into fairness testing, no ability to enforce responsible-gambling tools, and no recourse when a player is refused a withdrawal.

In practice it is one of the hardest numbers in the industry to pin down. Regulators can see exactly what the licensed side handles, because licensees report it. The offshore side, by definition, reports nothing. Estimates are assembled from payment-processor data, traffic analysis, survey responses and modelling, and each of those methods carries substantial uncertainty. When you see a channelization figure quoted anywhere in the world, it is an estimate built on assumptions, not a measurement — and reasonable analysts produce meaningfully different numbers from the same market.

Why Canada's structure makes it harder

Gambling in Canada is regulated province by province, a legacy of the 1985 Criminal Code amendments that handed the provinces authority over gaming conducted and managed within their borders. That fragmentation has consequences that a single national regulator would not face.

Different models, different results

Ontario opened a competitive commercial market in 2022, allowing private operators to apply for licences and compete. Alberta has since moved toward its own open framework. Most other provinces continue to run a single government-operated site, which is the model British Columbia, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces have used for years. A monopoly model can regulate its one operator perfectly and still see a great deal of local money leave for offshore sites, simply because one product cannot satisfy every preference.

That is the trade-off at the heart of the debate. A competitive market gives players enough choice, enough game variety and enough promotional value that they have less reason to look elsewhere — but it also normalises commercial gambling in a way monopoly markets do not. A monopoly keeps the commercial footprint small but concedes a share of demand to operators nobody can supervise. Neither is obviously correct, and the provinces have genuinely disagreed about which risk matters more. We traced how the different provincial approaches compare across the country in our coverage of Canada's regulated online casino landscape.

The tension nobody can resolve

Here is the structural problem. Every measure a regulator adds to protect players makes the licensed product slightly less attractive relative to the unlicensed one. Mandatory deposit limits, verification requirements, advertising restrictions, bonus rules, reality checks, cooling-off periods — each is defensible on its own terms, and each represents friction that offshore sites simply do not impose.

Push protections too far and you drive the very players you were trying to protect toward operators with no protections at all. Push them too lightly and you have licensed a market that fails the people it was supposed to safeguard. Regulators in every open market in the world are running this calibration in real time, with imperfect data on whether they have it right.

  • Advertising limits reduce gambling's cultural footprint but also reduce awareness of which sites are actually licensed.
  • Strict verification blocks underage and excluded players but adds sign-up friction that unlicensed sites skip.
  • Bonus restrictions curb aggressive inducements but remove a visible reason to choose the regulated option.
  • Deposit and loss limits protect vulnerable players but can push high-stakes players offshore entirely.
  • Payment blocking is the bluntest tool available, and its effectiveness is heavily disputed wherever it has been tried.

What actually moves the number

International experience suggests the biggest driver of channelization is not enforcement but product. Players go where the experience is good. Markets that licensed a broad range of operators, allowed a competitive game catalogue and kept payments fast have generally captured a high share of local play. Markets that licensed a narrow product, or that layered on restrictions faster than players could absorb them, have generally struggled.

Enforcement still matters at the edges. Payment blocking, domain-level action, advertising prohibitions on unlicensed brands and pressure on affiliate marketers all raise the friction of reaching an offshore site. But none of them removes demand. They redirect it, and only if there is somewhere acceptable for it to go.

Affiliate regulation has become a notable front in this fight. Canadian standards now hold marketing partners to requirements around promoting only licensed operators in regulated provinces, which changes what players see when they search. Sites like this one cover the market accordingly, and our operator reviews flag licensing status prominently for exactly that reason.

What it means if you are the one placing the bet

Strip away the policy language and channelization comes down to a practical question about recourse. If a licensed operator refuses your withdrawal, there is a regulator with authority over that company, a complaints process, and a licence they do not want to lose. If an offshore operator refuses your withdrawal, your options are the operator's own internal process and whatever leverage public complaint gives you.

That is the real difference, and it is worth more than a marginally better bonus. The game fairness testing, the segregation of player funds, the dispute resolution, the self-exclusion that actually works across operators — these exist on the licensed side because someone can enforce them. Players in newly regulated provinces should understand what their own market now offers; our guide to Alberta sports betting walks through what provincial regulation changed there.

Where this goes next

The likely trajectory is more provinces watching the open-market results and deciding whether to follow. Each one that opens expands the licensed share of Canadian play mechanically, simply by converting demand that was previously unsupervised. Whether the protections travel with it, and whether they are calibrated well enough to keep players on the licensed side, is the question the next few years will answer.

For players, the practical advice is unchanged and unglamorous. Check that the site you are using is licensed where you live. Understand that the friction you encounter at a regulated operator is the visible part of a system that exists to give you somewhere to turn. And keep following the market as it shifts — our industry news coverage tracks provincial developments as they land.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
